ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Pulmonology Referral — Elizabeth Barrett Browning — True-date frame: synthetic events are moved into the patient's historical lifetime. Codes, instruments, and treatments remain modern and are anachronistic.

code.originalText: New patient visit for chronic cough with blood-streaked sputum, a long-term opioid prescription, and grief, with tuberculosis testing and urgent pulmonology referral

text.paragraph: Chronic productive cough for several years with occasional streaks of blood in the sputum and breathlessness on stairs, in a thin 39-year-old poet who had a chest illness with blood in the sputum about eight years ago and has taken prescribed oral morphine for many years. Please help exclude tuberculosis and nontuberculous mycobacterial disease, establish the diagnosis (bronchiectasis is suspected), plan its care, and advise on morphine and her lungs. [S]

Urgency: Urgent, within one week; she is stable, with streaks of blood only, and has been told to call 911 or go to the emergency department for more than a few teaspoons of blood, blood with breathlessness, or chest pain. She is masking in shared spaces until the smears are back. [S]

list.item: Can tuberculosis be excluded, and when can she stop masking?
What is the cause of her cough and blood-streaked sputum: bronchiectasis, nontuberculous mycobacterial disease, or another lesion such as a congenital malformation or a tumour?
If this is bronchiectasis, what work-up for its cause and what treatment do you advise, including airway clearance and an exacerbation plan?
How does long-term morphine affect her lung disease, and does the pulmonary view favour any change in the dose?
When should blood in the sputum send her to the emergency department, and does she need bronchial artery treatment now?

text.paragraph: Daily cough with three to four tablespoons of yellow sputum, worse in winter, for several years; streaks of blood every few weeks, the last a week ago; breathless on one flight of stairs; palpitations at night. About eight years ago she had an illness with blood in the sputum after which she has largely stayed indoors; her physicians then thought it an affection of the lungs rather than consumption. A serious illness at about fifteen with a spinal injury, after which an opiate was prescribed; she now takes morphine sulfate oral solution 10 mg twice daily (20 mg a day), unchanged for years, for cough, sleeplessness and palpitations, and has never taken more than prescribed. The prescription monitoring program shows one prescriber and one pharmacy; a urine drug test today is consistent with morphine only; naloxone has been prescribed. DSM-5-TR assessment: no opioid use disorder; tolerance and withdrawal on prescribed use do not count. No tobacco, alcohol or sedatives. Prolonged grief disorder after her brother's drowning five years ago (PHQ-9 12, no suicidal ideation; safety plan in place). No known allergy. Today: weight 41.5 kg (BMI 16.8), blood pressure 102/64, pulse 96, respirations 18, temperature 36.9 °C, oxygen saturation 96% on room air; coarse crackles at the left base and mid-zone; no clubbing. Hemoglobin 12.3 g/dL, white cells 8.6 with eosinophils 0.21 x10^3/uL, platelets 352; CRP 8.4 mg/L; sodium 139, potassium 4.1 mmol/L, creatinine 0.66 mg/dL; 25-hydroxyvitamin D 15 ng/mL. Three sputum samples for acid-fast smear, NAAT and culture, a routine culture, an interferon-gamma release assay and an HIV test are pending [S]

list.item: She has coughed for years and lately sees streaks of blood; she wants to know whether it is consumption. [S]
She worries that the morphine she has taken for so long is harming her, but fears being made to stop it. [S]
She wants to keep writing, and to be able to think of her brother without being overwhelmed. [S]

text.paragraph: Historical basis. These claims are historical evidence, not findings from a modern examination.

list.item: Elizabeth Barrett was born on 6 March 1806 at Coxhoe Hall, about five miles south of Durham, the eldest child of Edward and Mary Moulton Barrett, and the eldest of twelve children; her father had added the surname Barrett as heir to his maternal grandfather's Jamaican estates. [D]

In 1821, while the family lived at Hope End in Herefordshire, she was seriously ill and went to the spa at Gloucester for treatment in June, returning to Hope End in May 1822; she later wrote, 'At fifteen I nearly died.' [D]

Her first editor reported that at about fifteen she injured her spine, by one account in a fall while saddling her pony, and by her son's statement through a strain while tightening the pony's girths, the injury not being discovered for some time; the editor judged that it contributed to the general weakness of health to which she was always subject. [D]
After the illness of 1821 she took opium by medical prescription, developing a lifelong habit. [D]

In 1838, after the family settled at 50 Wimpole Street, her health was in a very serious condition owing to the breaking of a blood-vessel; from then until her marriage she lived the life of an invalid. [D]
In August 1838 she moved to Torquay for her health, where her favourite brother Edward ('Bro') was her chief companion. [D]

On 11 July 1840 her brother Edward and two friends went sailing and did not return; the bodies were found three days later after a boat foundered in Babbacombe Bay. Her first editor wrote that she had the misery of thinking it was to attend on her that he had come to Torquay, that the place became a memory from which she shrank, and that even the sound of the sea became a horror to her. [D]

Her health suffered after the drowning; in the autumn of 1840 Mary Russell Mitford did not dare expect more than a few months of life for her, but she slowly gathered strength through the winter and returned to London in September 1841. [D]
Her brother Sam died in Jamaica in February 1840. [D]
Her mother died on 1 October 1828 after a last illness. [D]

On 2 October 1841 she wrote to H. S. Boyd that her case was 'not tubercular consumption, not what is called a decline, but an affection of the lungs which leans towards it', that a blood-vessel had broken three years before, and that four physicians, two experienced in diseases of the chest, agreed in that opinion. [D]
Her correspondence with the poet Robert Browning began in January 1845. [D]

list.item: Poet and translator; writes most days, lying on a sofa in her room with her papers on her knee; publishes widely and keeps up a large correspondence with other writers [S]
Never married; no children; lives on an upper floor of her father's house in the city with several of her siblings; a small dog is her constant companion [S]
Tobacco: never. Alcohol: none. No other drugs. Takes her prescribed morphine solution as directed and keeps it in her room [S]
Activity: rarely goes outdoors, and in winter stays in a warmed room for months; walks within the house [S]
Bereavement: her closest brother drowned in a sailing accident five years ago at the seaside town where she had gone for her health; she has not spoken of it with anyone since [S]
Supports: her writing, her correspondents, her sisters' company, and a strong sense of humour; financially independent through a legacy [S]

Evaluation of chronic cough with blood-streaked sputum: three sputum samples at least eight hours apart, one early morning, for acid-fast smear, nucleic acid amplification and mycobacterial culture (including nontuberculous mycobacteria) and routine bacterial culture; interferon-gamma release assay and HIV test; blood count, CRP and metabolic panel; CT of the chest within a week; a mask in shared spaces until the smears are negative; call 911 or go to the emergency department for more than a few teaspoons of blood, blood with breathlessness, or chest pain. Guideline: British Thoracic Society Guideline for Bronchiectasis in Adults (2019); Official American Thoracic Society/Infectious Diseases Society of America/Centers for Disease Control and Prevention Clinical Practice Guidelines: Diagnosis of Tuberculosis in Adults and Children (2017); Treatment of Nontuberculous Mycobacterial Pulmonary Disease: An Official ATS/ERS/ESCMID/IDSA Clinical Practice Guideline (2020) [S]

Long-term opioid therapy review: prescription monitoring program checked (one prescriber, one pharmacy), urine drug test consistent with morphine only, naloxone prescribed and taught, no benzodiazepines or other sedatives, DSM-5-TR assessment (no opioid use disorder), dose continued unchanged with no forced taper, benefits and harms reviewed at every visit and at least every three months, the monitoring program checked with every prescription, and buprenorphine offered if opioid use disorder ever develops. Guideline: CDC Clinical Practice Guideline for Prescribing Opioids for Pain, United States, 2022 (2022); Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition, Text Revision (DSM-5-TR): opioid use disorder and prolonged grief disorder criteria (2022) [S]

Prolonged grief disorder therapy with the clinic psychologist, weekly for sixteen sessions, by video at first so she need not travel; PHQ-9 at every visit. Guideline: Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition, Text Revision (DSM-5-TR): opioid use disorder and prolonged grief disorder criteria (2022); Shear MK, et al. Optimizing Treatment of Complicated Grief: A Randomized Clinical Trial (2016); CMID: Clinical Monitoring Intelligence Database, depression and osteoporosis monographs (2026) [S]

Collaborative safety plan with warning signs, coping steps, people to contact, the clinic number and the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline; morphine kept in a locked box with only the current bottle out; safety reviewed at every visit. Guideline: CDC Clinical Practice Guideline for Prescribing Opioids for Pain, United States, 2022 (2022); VA/DoD Clinical Practice Guideline for Assessment and Management of Patients at Risk for Suicide (2024) [S]

Bone and nutrition: vitamin D3 1819 units daily with a recheck at twelve weeks; DXA for low weight, vitamin D deficiency, limited weight-bearing and long-term opioid therapy; calcium-rich foods, small frequent meals and an oral supplement drink with the clinic dietitian; weight at every visit. Guideline: CMID: Clinical Monitoring Intelligence Database, depression and osteoporosis monographs (2026) [S]
